CAPITAL PUNISHMENT. " Ii was • maxim of his," quotes Thaokeray from one of Fielding's novels, "that no man can descend below himself, in doing any act which may contribute to protect an innocent person, or to bring a rogue to the gallows." " 'I he moralist of that age," continues the satirist, "had no compunction, you see, he had not begun to be sceptical about the theory of punishment, and thought the hanging of a thief was a spectacle for edifi- cation. Masters sent their apprentices, fathers took their children to see Jack Shep- herd or Jonathan Wild hanged; and it was as undoubting subscribers to this moral law that Fielding wrote and liogarth painted," No one acquaiuted with the social character- istic. of the earlier half of the 13th century can feel any surprise at this. The duello . was then the recognised mode of assuaging the pangs of "wounded honour," and to wash out an insult in the blood of a foe was just as laudable as to throw half-pence to a beggar. We have left that order of things • good way behind us, but the ler talionie has its roots too deeply struck in our nature to permit of a humanitarian regime, pure and simple. No doubt thinking people now admit that man's vocation is to "Move upward, working out the beast, and let the ape and tiger die," but the homicidal frenzy is etill very for from being an exceptional malady. War panics are not yet out of fashion. Lynch law finds favour with city mobs occasionally. Tragedies are still enacted in gaming rooms by "gentlemen," and in pot houses by " cads " ; for it seems natural to undisciplined minds to thirst for vengeance under real or mipposed injury. and to cry out like Sim lappertil, for "gore." Nay, society at large, at the close of the nineteenth Christian century, clings to the dictum of the obsolete Judaic code, 'whose sheddeth mane blood, by man shall his blood be shed." no it comes to pass that a debate on a motion to revise, and an amendment to do away with, the existing law under which convicted murderers are strangled, results in a re-endorsement of the sanguinary prac- tice by large Parliamentary majorities. The proposal of Mr. Basso to substitute life- servitude for the death penalty was grounded upon considerations of wise expediency, as well as upon principles which must in the nature of things, meet with more general acceptance as the advancing intelligence of mankind applies itself to the ealu ion of moral problems. "The great object of punishment is not to avenge, but to prevent crime, and to make the criminal a better men." The juriets disallow the idea of vindictive punishment, but they are apt to take the virtue out of this concession by arguing, as the Attorney-General did the other night, that terrible penalties are needed as deterrents. The sheep stealer used to be hanged, as a judge once remarked, not be- cause he had etolen a sheep, but in order that sheep might not be stolen. Now, though statistics are far from being an infalli- ble guide, it is obvious that to meet this peculiarly-legal style of argument it is only necessary to show that the abolition of capital punishment in other civilised countriee has ! not been followed by an increase of mur. ders, whereas hanging appears to have anything but a deterring effect upon the classes which furnish homicidal criminals in this land where life is reputed to be so "sacred." The proof that these things are so is readily producible, and it cameo con- viction to most unprejudiced minds. In . tdolladd and Belgium life is not least_ but more secure than in this country. In Michi- gan the knife and pistol are not, certainly, in greater request than in other States. Even Portugal and s uscany can safely diepenve with the hangman and the guillotine. The truth womb to be that the certainty and no; the severity of punishment is the most in- fluential deterrent when passion dictates to . reason, and consequences pans in swift re- view before the would-be homicide. The . chances of escape are many. There is the unwillingness of witnessea to "deliver the man to death," if, as commonly happens, a fit of rage has led him to imbrue his hands in a neighbour's blood, lhen, there are tne chances of escape which the forms and tech- nicalities of the law now offer to the criminal whose own tile is in the balance. lid is warned not to confess, and often advised to withdraw his plea of "guilty." Add ti, this the danger (a very real one, as the number of known cases attests) of hanging the wrong person; and the hope of reprieve which so olten veils the terrors of the fatal hour until the toll if the bell summons the miserable wretch to the spot where .the hangman and his cord await him.—you have a chapter ot 0011tingences winch may well lead the callous and the thoughttul alike to review the whole subject land ask themselves whether the England el to-day cannot fence human life about with a higher consecration, and— while setting a mark of dread upon the man- slayer —which will more and more diminish the fascination of vengeful violence—anewer theory of the brother's blood with a whisper of better things. All this, and much more, found eloquent expression from lips which have not been given to lavish talking of late; but which have only to open on questions of high social and moral significance, to arrest the con- sciences and persuade the hesitating judg- ments of countless thousands in the anglish.. speaking world. In tones now solemn, now eo,7fsre, now sympathetic, Mr. Bright re- viewed the whole subject in the light of history and experience, lie dwelt upon the unanimous damnation of the existing law by the Commission Z.`.! 1866 tie Gamily noticed the abandonment of the "Scripture argument" by the advocates of ' the gallows. Ile showed that when public °amid°oo ceased, the terror which the death-penalty was imagined to inspire in lawless breasts would largely pass away. The Attorney-General had to submit to a preleotion from that prophetic tongue, and once again learn the ealutary lesson that there were spiritual facts and pleas undreamt ,of in Ids forensic philosophy. The analysis Of the moral elements which enter into the . problem was masterly, as might have been anticipated. In former times they told you all about the crowd, and how the street was filled with spectators, but now, in a space cot perhaps half the size of this room, they see every line of the convict's countenance, they see his troubled eyes, the pallor on his cheek, the teiror in every limb, and all that is given with all the embellishments which news- paper writers are so able to add, and these details are carried into every house, and I believe at this moment your executions are exerting an influence as evil, and I believe more evil, upon the public mind than they . did in times when they were under the canopy of heaven and before the faces of thousands of the people." div.p: THE WAR.

Since our last issue events of great impor- tance have taken place at the seat of war. An important battle was fought on the 15th between Mukhtar Pasha's right wing and the left wing of the Russian army at Adage], Kind. The contest raged for several hours, and the Turkish General, Mehemet Pasha, was slain. Both sides Claim the victory. From the Danube it is reported that the Russian head-quarters have been removed from Plojesti to Alexandria,_ and there is a rumour that the Russians began to cross the Danube at Satanoyo, opposite Isaias& on Wednesday morning at three o'clock. Rus- sia has invited Austria to make military preparations for the purpose of preventing the utter annihilation of siontenegru by the overwhelmingonslaught of the Turks.
